migrationNotes: SPINE: Start with a friend's offhand advice and keep asking what is holding it up: first the conclusion and the fact offered for it, then the unstated rule that links them, then where an opponent would push, then the parts a careful speaker adds to defend against that push.

lesson.title: Claim, grounds and warrant

steps.headline: What an argument is made of

lead.text: An argument is an attempt to get someone to accept a conclusion by giving them a reason. Take a coach choosing a team: “Pick Mia, because she scored twenty goals this season.” Two things are on the table. The conclusion the coach wants accepted, “Pick Mia”, is the claim. The fact offered to support it, that she scored twenty goals, is the grounds.

To find the claim in any passage, ask which statement the others are reasons for. To find the grounds, ask what the speaker points to as evidence, which is usually a fact you could check or something observed. The claim can come first or last. Words such as “because”, “since” and “so” often sit between the two and show which way the reasoning runs.

afterFigure.text: Grounds alone do not make an argument. Twenty goals says nothing about picking Mia until a further idea is added, and that idea is the next stop.

statements.text: Pick Mia for the team.
Mia scored twenty goals this season.
Every light in the house is on.
Someone is at home.

lead.text: Three statements about a bridge. Ask which one the other two are reasons for.

reveal.text: You looked for the conclusion. The claim is the statement the others are reasons for: here, closing the bridge.

statements.text: Inspectors found cracks in two of the bridge's four main girders.
The bridge should close to lorries.
A structure with damaged load-bearing girders should not carry heavy loads.
The museum should open late every Thursday.
Attendance doubled on the four Thursdays it stayed open late.
A change that doubles attendance justifies its staffing cost.
The trial lasted only four weeks, so the rise may not last.

steps.headline: The rule that links the two

lead.text: Look again at the coach's argument. Twenty goals is a fact about Mia, and “Pick Mia” is an instruction. A fact cannot give an instruction by itself. Something else carries you from one to the other, and it is a general belief the coach holds: players who score a lot help a team. Nobody says it aloud, because it seems too obvious to need saying.

That belief is the warrant, the general rule that licenses the step from grounds to claim. The word comes from the same root as a search warrant, a document that gives someone the right to act. Grounds are particular and the warrant is general, and the warrant is usually left unstated.

afterFigure.text: Because the warrant is hidden, it is where arguments are often weakest. An opponent might reply that goals scored against weak teams prove little. Nobody can make that reply until the rule has been written out.

statements.text: Mia scored twenty goals this season.
Pick Mia for the team.
Players who score a lot help a team.
Every light in the house is on.
Someone is at home.
People switch lights on when they are in.

lead.text: Back to your friend and her dog. Separate what she said from what she assumed.

steps.headline: Label the parts of: “Rain is forecast, so take a coat, since forecasts are usually right.”

lead.text: Use the three questions from the last screens.

workedSteps.text: Find the conclusion. “Take a coat” is what the writer wants accepted, so it is the claim.
Find the fact offered for it. “Rain is forecast” is a particular fact, so it is the grounds.
Ask what rule links the two. “Forecasts are usually right” is general, so it is the warrant.

steps.headline: Label the rule behind: “His fingerprints were on the knife, so he handled it.”

lead.text: The claim and the grounds are given. The rule between them is the part left out.

reveal.text: Writing the rule out shows what the argument assumes. Once it is written, a lawyer can ask whether prints show handling at the relevant time.

workedSteps.text: The claim is “he handled the knife”.
The grounds are “his fingerprints were on the knife”.
Name the unstated rule that links the two.

statements.text: The defendant's fingerprints were on the knife.
The defendant handled the knife.
Fingerprints on an object show that a person touched it.
It is Saturday lunchtime.
The café will be busy.
Cafés are busy at Saturday lunchtime.

lead.text: Once a warrant is written out you can test it. In the knife argument nobody disputes the fingerprints, because they were found and photographed. A defence lawyer attacks the rule instead. Prints show that someone touched the knife at some time, but the argument needs them to show that the defendant held it during the crime. The grounds are untouched, and the argument is weaker all the same.

That is why it pays to name the warrant when you read an argument. Disagreeing with the grounds means arguing about facts. Disagreeing with the warrant means arguing about what the facts prove, and that is where most real arguments are won or lost. A careful speaker knows this, and builds some defences into the argument in advance.

afterFigure.text: The next screen shows two of those defences, which are small additions that change how far an argument claims to reach.

diagram.alt: The knife argument drawn as grounds, claim and warrant. In the second view the grounds are marked as undisputed and the warrant is marked as the weak point.
diagram.caption: A defence lawyer leaves the grounds alone and goes for the warrant. Use the buttons to see where.

lead.text: A careful speaker admits the limits of a claim before an opponent can point them out, and there are two ways to do it. A qualifier says how strongly the claim is made, with words such as “in most cases”, “very likely” or “presumably”. A rebuttal names the conditions under which the claim would fail, and it often opens with “unless”.

Take “The ferry will in most cases sail on time, unless fog closes the harbour.” The qualifier is “in most cases” and the rebuttal is “unless fog closes the harbour”. Neither weakens the argument. Both make it harder to knock down, because the exceptions an opponent would raise have already been granted. An argument with no qualifier claims to hold every time, and a single exception then breaks it.

afterFigure.text: Qualifiers and rebuttals are the speaker's honesty built into the argument. They say how sure the speaker is and what would change that.

statements.text: The harbour has been clear all week.
In most cases,
The ferry will sail on time.
Unless fog closes the harbour.
Mia scored twenty goals this season.
Very likely,
Mia will help the team.
Unless an injury keeps her out.

lead.text: One sentence holds both a qualifier and a rebuttal. Read for the word that measures how sure the writer is.

reveal.text: You separated the two. A qualifier and a rebuttal concede in advance the exceptions an opponent would raise, so the claim is harder to knock down.

statements.text: Harriet leads every poll by eight points.
Probably.
Harriet will win the election.
Unless rain keeps her supporters at home.
The air pressure is falling fast.
Very likely.
It will rain tomorrow.
Unless the front stalls over the coast.

lead.text: There is one more part. A warrant is a rule, and a rule can itself be doubted. A speaker who expects doubt supplies backing, which is support for the warrant itself. Backing differs from grounds. Grounds support the claim, and backing supports the rule that links the grounds to it.

A doctor argues that a patient should take an antibiotic because the infection is bacterial. The warrant is that antibiotics treat bacterial infections. The backing is the clinical trials behind that rule, which nobody needs to cite until someone doubts the rule.

afterFigure.text: A full argument can have six parts, and you will rarely meet all of them in one passage. The skill is to notice which are present and which are missing.

statements.text: The infection is bacterial.
Almost certainly,
The patient should take an antibiotic.
Antibiotics treat bacterial infections.
Clinical trials show that antibiotics clear bacterial infections.
Unless the patient is allergic.
The defendant's fingerprints were on the knife.
The defendant handled the knife.
Fingerprints on an object show that a person touched it.
Forensic studies show that ridge patterns are individual and transfer by contact.

lead.text: Label each statement by the job it does. A particular observation is grounds, a general rule linking it to the conclusion is the warrant, and an “unless” clause is a rebuttal.

reveal.text: Sorting by job shows the shape: a fact, a general rule, a conclusion and an exception. Only one statement is a general rule.

statements.text: Sales fell 20% in the month after the price rise.
Customers buy less of a product when its price rises.
The price should return to its old level.
Unless costs have risen faster than sales have fallen.
The council should plant trees on Gale Street.
Gale Street is hotter in summer than streets that have trees.
Shade lowers the temperature of a street.
Unless the roots would damage the pipes below.

lesson.orientation: Take an argument apart with Toulmin's model: the claim and the grounds offered for it, the warrant that links them, the qualifiers and rebuttals that limit it.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh text after a delay.

blocks.text: Your friend leans across the table and says, “Get a dog: mine makes me so happy.” She means it kindly, and it sounds like a reason. You nod, and then you find yourself hesitating, though you could not yet say what is bothering you.

Most persuasion has this shape. There is a piece of advice, a fact offered to back it, and a connection that nobody mentions because it seems obvious. When the connection is sound you never notice it. When it is shaky you feel the shakiness without knowing where it comes from.

In 1958 the philosopher Stephen Toulmin offered a way to find it. This lesson takes his method and uses it on small cases: a bridge inspection, a fingerprint on a knife, a museum's opening hours. You will learn to name the parts of an argument and to see where it can be attacked.

intro.promise: By the end you'll split an argument into claim, grounds and warrant, and spot the qualifiers and rebuttals that limit it.

recap.keyIdea: Every argument has a claim, grounds and a warrant that links them. Qualifiers and rebuttals limit it, and backing supports the warrant.

blocks.text: You picked the claim in a bridge argument and counted what your friend had said aloud and what she had left unsaid. You named the warrant behind a fingerprint case, found the qualifier in an election forecast and numbered the warrant in a pricing argument.

recap.nextHook: Structure is only part of persuasion, and the next lesson begins with three people who each have one sentence to win your trust as you choose a guide for a mountain trip.

questions.prompt: Three statements: 'Inspectors found cracks in two of the bridge's four main girders.' 'The bridge should close to lorries.' 'A structure with damaged load-bearing girders should not carry heavy loads.' Which is the claim?
hints: Ask which statement the others are reasons for.

acceptedIdeas: The bridge should close to lorries.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'The bridge should close to lorries' is the conclusion the other two statements are offered to support.

choices.label: Inspectors found cracks in two of the bridge's four main girders.
The bridge should close to lorries.
A structure with damaged load-bearing girders should not carry heavy loads.

questions.onCorrect: The bridge should close to lorries: the other two statements are offered as its reasons.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a fact offered in support. Ask which statement the others are reasons for.
That is a general rule linking fact to conclusion, so it supports something else.

questions.prompt: Grounds: 'The defendant's fingerprints were on the knife.' Claim: 'The defendant handled the knife.' What is Toulmin's name for the unstated rule 'Fingerprints on an object show that a person touched it'?
hints: The element authorises the step from evidence to conclusion; the same word names a document that authorises a search.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The warrant: the general principle that authorises the move from these grounds to this claim.

questions.onCorrect: The warrant is the general principle that authorises the move from these grounds to this claim.

misconceptions.feedback: The claim is the conclusion, here the statement about handling. Name the rule that links the fact to it.
The grounds are the fingerprints themselves. The question asks for the rule behind the step.
Backing supports that rule. The question asks for the rule itself.

questions.prompt: In 'Harriet will probably win, unless rain keeps her supporters at home', which single word is the qualifier?
hints: Find the word that measures how confident the claim is.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Probably' limits the force of the claim; 'unless rain keeps her supporters at home' is the rebuttal, the condition under which it fails.

questions.onCorrect: “Probably” limits the force of the claim. The “unless” clause is the rebuttal.

misconceptions.feedback: That part names what could go wrong. Find the word that measures how sure the writer is.

questions.prompt: Statements: (1) Sales fell 20% in the month after the price rise. (2) Customers buy less of a product when its price rises. (3) The price should return to its old level. (4) Unless costs have risen faster than sales have fallen. Give the number of the statement that is the warrant.
hints: Find the claim first: the statement the others support.
Find the observed fact; that is the grounds.
The warrant is a general rule rather than a particular fact.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Statement 2 is the warrant: a general rule linking the sales figure (grounds, statement 1) to the pricing claim (statement 3). Statement 4 is the rebuttal.

questions.onCorrect: Statement 2 is the warrant: a general rule linking the sales figure to the pricing claim.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a particular observed fact, so it supplies the grounds.
That is what the writer wants accepted: the claim.
That names exceptions that would limit the argument, so it is a rebuttal.

questions.prompt: Statements: (1) The museum should open late every Thursday. (2) Attendance doubled on the four Thursdays it stayed open late. (3) A change that doubles attendance justifies its staffing cost. (4) The trial lasted only four weeks, so the rise may not last. Give the number of the statement that supplies the grounds.
hints: Find the statement the others support.
Grounds are particular observed facts, not general rules.
The last statement limits the argument rather than supporting it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Statement 2 supplies the grounds: an observed fact. Statement 1 is the claim, 3 the warrant and 4 a rebuttal.

questions.onCorrect: Statement 2 is an observed fact, so it supplies the grounds for the claim in statement 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what the others support, so it is the claim.
That is a general rule, not an observed fact.
That limits the argument. It does not support it.

questions.prompt: A writer supports the warrant 'Damaged load-bearing girders should not carry heavy loads' by citing the national bridge inspection code. In Toulmin's model, what is that support called?
hints: The support is aimed at the rule, not at the conclusion.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Backing: support for the warrant itself, as opposed to grounds, which support the claim.

questions.onCorrect: Backing supports the warrant itself, as opposed to grounds, which support the claim.

misconceptions.feedback: Grounds support the claim. This support is aimed at the rule behind it.
A qualifier limits how strongly the claim is made. It supports nothing.

questions.prompt: Your friend says “Get a dog: mine makes me so happy.” How many of these does she say aloud? (1) You should get a dog. (2) Her dog makes her happy. (3) What makes her happy will make you happy.
hints: Read her exact words, one statement at a time.
Which statements can you find in what she said?
One statement is a belief that her advice relies on.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: statements 1 and 2. Statement 3 is the belief her advice depends on, and she never says it.

questions.onCorrect: Two: her advice and her reason. The belief that links them is unstated, yet her advice only follows if it holds.

misconceptions.feedback: Read her words again. One of these is a belief she assumes without saying.
She says more than the advice. Check what reason she gives.
She says at least her advice. Check each statement against her words.

questions.prompt: “The pavement is wet, so it has rained.” Which words give the grounds?
hints: Which part can you check by looking?
questions.onCorrect: The grounds are the observed fact. “It has rained” is the claim, and the link between them is the warrant.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the conclusion drawn from the fact, so it is the claim. Find the fact itself.
That would be a general rule linking fact to conclusion. Grounds are the particular fact.

questions.prompt: Why is “forecasts are usually right” a warrant and not grounds?

acceptedIdeas: It is a general rule that links the fact to the claim.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is a general rule linking the particular fact to the claim.

choices.label: It is a general rule that links the fact to the claim.
It comes last in the sentence.

questions.onCorrect: A warrant is a general rule. Grounds are the particular fact it lets you rely on.

misconceptions.feedback: Position does not decide the role. Ask whether the statement is a fact or a rule.
A qualifier can sit in any statement. The question is what job the statement does.

questions.prompt: In “The tournament will almost certainly go ahead, unless the pitch floods”, which part is the rebuttal?
hints: Which part says when the claim would not hold?
questions.onCorrect: The rebuttal names the condition under which the claim would fail.

misconceptions.feedback: That words how sure the writer is. Look for the part that says what would make the claim fail.
That is the claim itself. A rebuttal limits it from outside.

questions.prompt: In “Buses are usually on time, unless snow falls”, which word opens the rebuttal?
hints: Which word introduces what could stop the claim holding?
questions.onCorrect: The rebuttal names the condition under which the claim would fail, and here it opens with “unless”.

misconceptions.feedback: “Usually” measures how often the claim holds. A rebuttal names what could defeat it.
That is part of the claim. A rebuttal limits it from outside.
